screens.title: Designing UI and Best Practices for dApps
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn how user interfaces for decentralized applications differ from traditional web apps and why UI matters for adoption. A dApp user manages a wallet, pays gas, and waits for confirmations. These elements introduce delays and potential confusion, so your interface must provide clear guidance and prevent costly mistakes. We will look at state-driven rendering, feedback for pending and failed transactions, network mismatch handling, and accessibility considerations. For example, telling a user that a transaction is pending and disabling repeat actions prevents duplicate transactions and wasted gas. A common misconception is that web UI patterns alone are sufficient; in practice you must surface blockchain-specific status and educate without overwhelming the user. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design screens for disconnected, connected, wrong network, and pending transaction states, and implement clear visual and textual cues that reduce user risk. Think about the last time an app left you waiting without context; that frustration is amplified when money or irreversible actions are involved. How will you give your users confidence when the network is slow?

keyIdea.title: Why dApp UX is different
keyIdea.text: Blockchain latency, wallet flows, gas costs, and immutability require state-aware UI and explicit feedback to prevent errors and build trust.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Designing UI for dApps
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Designing UI and Best Practices for dApps

Anticipate wallet flows, transaction delays, and network mismatches. Build trust with clear feedback and state-aware visuals.

Connect Flow
Prompt to connect wallet and explain why connection is required.
Transaction Status
Show pending, confirmed, and failed states with context and actions.
Network Handling
Detect wrong network and guide users to switch safely.
Key Idea
Treat blockchain steps as first-class states in the UI, not background events.
Common Mistake
Assuming instant confirmations and failing to disable repeat actions.
In this lesson
State-driven UI, feedback, accessibility, and secure patterns
You will see patterns that reduce user friction when wallets and network latency create delays. Focus on clear language, disabled controls during processing, and explicit error messages that help recovery.
Coming up
Hands-on code walkthrough for App.jsx, conditional rendering examples, testing states, and accessibility checks you can apply immediately.
Explore Key Topics
Connect flow: why a clear connect prompt reduces confusion.
Transaction status: preventing duplicate sends and showing confirmations.
Network handling: detect and guide when user is on wrong chain.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this module you will master four practical skills that improve dApp usability. First, you will identify unique UX challenges in decentralized apps, such as wallet interactions, gas fees, and transaction latency, and explain why these require different patterns than typical web apps. Second, you will implement clear feedback mechanisms for transactions: how to show pending, confirmed, and failed states with useful messaging and transaction hashes. Third, you will design state-aware interfaces for disconnected, connected-but-no-account, wrong-network, and pending transaction conditions so users always know what to do next. Fourth, you will apply general UI and accessibility best practices, such as semantic markup, color contrast, and keyboard navigation, to make your dApp trustworthy and inclusive. Each objective is measurable: you will add conditional rendering for connection and network, display transaction status, and validate accessibility checks. These skills reduce user error, prevent lost funds, and increase confidence in your dApp. Which objective matters most for your current project, and how will you prioritize it?

screens.title: Skills and Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson is focused on translating UX objectives into concrete outcomes you can test. You should be able to explain three interface states clearly to a teammate and implement them in code: disconnected, wrong network, and pending transaction. For example, a disconnected state displays an explanation and a prominent connect affordance; a wrong network state explains the mismatch and offers an explicit path to resolve it; a pending transaction state disables repeat actions and shows a transaction hash. These are measurable behaviors you can test by disconnecting your wallet or switching the network. Accessibility and responsive design are also part of success: using semantic elements, sufficient contrast, and keyboard reachable controls ensures broader adoption. A common misconception is that polished visuals alone equal good UX. In truth, reliable state handling and clear messaging are what prevent user harm and build trust. After completing exercises, ask yourself: can a new user recover from a failed transaction without developer help?

keyIdea.text: Success is measurable: distinct states, clear guidance, disabling risky actions, and accessibility checks.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Skills & Outcomes

Practical outcomes

You'll be able to implement and test connection and network checks, render transaction statuses, and run manual scenarios to validate behavior. These are operational, not just design goals.

Test Scenario
Disconnect wallet, reconnect, switch network, send a transaction, and observe disabled controls while pending.
Accessibility Check

Mnemonic

screens.title: dApp UX challenges
screens.narratorSegment: Decentralized applications introduce UX challenges that are not common in traditional web apps. At the core, users must manage a separate wallet, contend with gas costs, and accept that transactions are sometimes slow and irreversible. Start by defining the core claim: a dApp interface must treat blockchain interactions as first-class events. Concretely, that means surfacing wallet connection status, transaction lifecycle, and network identity, and making recovery paths explicit. For example, a user who sends a token transfer expects feedback; if the UI does nothing for thirty seconds, the user may retry and create duplicate transfers. A common misconception is to rely on default wallet modals and assume they are always sufficient. In reality, you must complement wallet prompts with in-app messages and disabled actions to prevent mistakes. Design patterns include clear labels, confirmation steps for risky actions, and an activity log or transaction history. The practical takeaway is to always ask: what could go wrong from the user's perspective, and how does the interface prevent or recover from that failure? That mindset will reorganize your priorities and make your dApp safer.

keyIdea.title: Treat blockchain events as first-class
keyIdea.text: Surface wallet, network, and transaction lifecycle explicitly to prevent confusion and errors.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › dApp UX challenges
Definition
dApp UX challenges are the interface problems that arise because users must connect wallets, wait for confirmations, and manage irreversible on-chain changes.
Wallet Interaction
Users approve transactions outside your UI. Your app must reflect approvals, rejections, and missing accounts.
Gas & Latency
Transactions take time and cost money. Show costs and prevent duplicate sends.
Immutability
Once on chain, state changes are final. Confirm intent and provide clear receipts.
Concrete Example
A token transfer UI should show estimated gas, require confirmation, display a pending indicator, and show the transaction hash with a link to a block explorer. If it fails due to insufficient allowance, show the revert reason and next steps.
Key Takeaway

Design for failure modes and delays. Clear feedback prevents mistakes and builds user trust.

Common Mistake

Assuming instant confirmation and not disabling repeat actions leads to duplicate transactions and wasted gas.

screens.title: Feedback mechanisms for transactions
screens.narratorSegment: Providing clear feedback during the transaction lifecycle is essential for user confidence. Describe the lifecycle: a transaction is initiated, sent to the network, may remain pending, then either confirms or reverts. For each stage, provide visual and textual cues. When pending, disable relevant controls, show a spinner, and display a short message with the transaction hash so the user can reference it. For confirmed transactions, show a success message with a green check and update the UI to reflect the new state. For failures, show a prominent error that explains why it failed when possible, for example insufficient allowance or user rejection. A concrete example: when a user updates a greeting on a contract, the UI should show Processing with a hash, then update the greeting on confirmation. A common misconception is to hide error details for security; instead, give clear, actionable messages while avoiding sensitive data. The practical takeaway is to treat transaction feedback as an ordered process with explicit transitions, and test each transition by simulating slow confirmations and revert scenarios. Feedback mechanisms for transactions means always show pending, success, and failure states with actionable messages and transaction identifiers.. In practical terms, design clear pending, confirmed, and failed states. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Explicit lifecycle feedback
keyIdea.text: Always show pending, success, and failure states with actionable messages and transaction identifiers.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Transaction Feedback
Lifecycle Steps
1. Transaction Sent — show spinner and transaction hash for tracing.
2. Pending — disable action controls to prevent duplicate sends.
3. Confirmed — success message, update UI state and show receipt.
4. Failed — show clear revert reason and recovery guidance.
Example
Updating a greeting: show processing and hash, then update greeting text when confirmed, or explain revert reason on failure.
Common Mistake
Keeping action buttons enabled while awaiting confirmation, which can produce duplicate transactions.
Design Patterns
  • Show transaction hash and short explanation immediately after send.
  • Use color and icons: spinner for pending, green for success, red for error.
  • Provide suggested next steps on failure, like checking allowance or gas settings.
Key Takeaway
Make each lifecycle stage explicit and test for slow confirmations and revert messages.

screens.title: dApp States: disconnected, connected, wrong network
screens.narratorSegment: A robust dApp recognizes and clearly communicates its operational state. The primary states to design for are disconnected, connected but no account, and wrong network. For a disconnected user, explain why a wallet connection is necessary and provide a clear call to action. For connected users with no selected account, prompt selection and explain the need for an active account. For wrong network scenarios, show a prominent warning and explain which network the dApp requires, for example a Sepolia testnet contract. Avoid surprising behavior like attempting to send a transaction on an unsupported network. A concrete example: if your dApp is deployed to Sepolia and the user is on Mainnet, display a warning message stating the mismatch and steps to switch. A key misconception is to rely solely on wallet modals; although wallets surface prompts, your app must guide the user before they attempt transactions. The practical takeaway is to code clear, recoverable states, and to test them by switching or disconnecting wallets until the flows are smooth and comprehensible. dApp States: disconnected, connected, wrong network means detect connection and network state early, guide users with clear messages, and prevent unsupported actions.. In practical terms, design patterns for each operational mode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: State-first UI
keyIdea.text: Detect connection and network state early, guide users with clear messages, and prevent unsupported actions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › dApp States
Disconnected
Explain why connection is required and what actions will be available once connected. Provide clear instructions on connecting a wallet and verifying an account selection.
Connected but no account
Detect and prompt the user to select an active account. Explain that multiple wallet profiles can be present and one must be chosen.
Wrong Network
Show the required network name and guide users to switch. Emphasize not to attempt transactions on an unsupported chain.
Example
If your contract is on Sepolia and a user is on Mainnet, display: Wrong Network. Please switch to Sepolia. Provide steps or instructions for the wallet switch process.
Key Takeaway
Make each state explicit and prevent the user from performing unsupported actions.
Misconception
Assuming the wallet alone will prevent wrong-network transactions. Your UI must detect and warn first.

screens.title: Conditional rendering patterns (App.jsx)
screens.narratorSegment: Structuring your application to react to wallet and network changes begins with conditional rendering. The pattern is simple: check for an account, then check for network correctness, and finally render the main dApp content. In practice, use a small state machine in your app that maps to disconnected, wrong network, pending, or ready. A concrete example is an App. jsx component that returns a connect prompt if no account is present, a network warning when the chain does not match your target, and the main interface otherwise. When a transaction is in flight, set an isMining flag and render processing indicators while disabling the relevant inputs. A common misconception is to tightly couple UI components with wallet logic; instead, keep wallet detection and UI rendering separated so you can test each state independently. When testing, simulate a slow network and observe whether buttons are disabled and whether the transaction hash is shown. This approach improves maintainability and prevents UI surprises when the wallet state changes asynchronously. Conditional rendering patterns (App.jsx) means use simple conditional checks for account, network, and transaction flags to render appropriate ui and prevent risky actions.. In practical terms, how to structure ui logic for connection and network states. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: State-driven rendering
keyIdea.text: Use simple conditional checks for account, network, and transaction flags to render appropriate UI and prevent risky actions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Conditional Rendering
Pattern
Check account presence, then network correctness, then render main content. Use flags like isMining to control input availability during transactions.
Example snippet (visual only)
{`// inside App.jsx render
if (!account) {
  // show connect prompt
} else if (network && network !== 'sepolia') {
  // show wrong network warning
} else {
  // main dApp UI
}

// When sending:
// set isMining true, disable inputs, show hash and spinner
`}
Key Takeaway
Separate detection logic from UI rendering so each state is testable and predictable.
Common Mistake
Mixing wallet callbacks into many components rather than centralizing state leads to inconsistent behavior.
Testing checklist
  • Disconnect wallet: does the connect prompt appear?
  • Switch network: is the wrong-network warning shown?
  • Send a transaction while simulating latency: are inputs disabled and hash shown?

screens.title: Handling pending transactions and disabling actions
screens.narratorSegment: Pending transactions are a distinct state that requires special handling in your dApp. Define the claim: while a transaction is pending, relevant controls should be disabled and the user should see an explicit processing indicator and a transaction identifier. A concrete example is disabling a Set Greeting button while an update is mining and displaying a message like Processing, transaction hash 0xabc... so the user can track it. This prevents duplicate submissions and wasted gas. A common misconception is that optimistic UI without disabling actions is acceptable; optimistic updates can be useful, but never rely on them alone for irreversible on-chain changes. Instead, combine optimistic updates with locked inputs and clear rollback or correction guidance if the transaction reverts. Implement visual cues such as dimmed controls, spinners, and a short explanation of why interactions are paused. The practical takeaway is to make the pending state obvious and informative so users understand that the app is waiting on the network rather than frozen or broken. Handling pending transactions and disabling actions means disable repeat actions, show processing indicators and transaction hash, and provide rollback guidance on failure.. In practical terms, prevent duplicate sends and show clear processing feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lock while pending
keyIdea.text: Disable repeat actions, show processing indicators and transaction hash, and provide rollback guidance on failure.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Pending Transactions
Why lock actions
Locking prevents users from sending identical requests while the first is still being processed, saving gas and avoiding confusion.
Show a spinner and message like Processing… with the transaction hash for traceability.
Disable actionable inputs that would create equivalent transactions.
On failure, show the revert reason and clarify recovery steps.
Concrete Example
When the user sets a greeting, set isMining true. Render Processing with hash and disable the greeting input until confirmation or failure.
Key Takeaway
Make pending visible and prevent duplicate actions to protect users and avoid wasted fees.

screens.title: Presenting transaction errors and revert reasons
screens.narratorSegment: When a transaction fails, the user needs a clear explanation and a path to recovery. Define the intent: display a prominent error that explains why the transaction reverted when possible, such as insufficient allowance or user rejection. For example, if a transfer fails because the user has not approved token allowance, show: Transaction reverted: Insufficient allowance, and provide next steps like granting allowance or checking token balance. Avoid exposing internal stack traces or sensitive data. A common misconception is that vague messages are safer; in fact, vague errors frustrate users and increase support requests. Instead, map revert reasons to helpful guidance and, when the exact reason is unknown, offer troubleshooting steps such as reviewing gas settings, checking balances, and consulting transaction history. The practical takeaway is to convert low-level revert signals into human-friendly advice so users know what to do next and can recover without developer intervention. Presenting transaction errors and revert reasons means translate revert reasons into clear guidance and recovery steps while avoiding raw internal errors.. In practical terms, provide actionable error messages without exposing sensitive data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Actionable errors
keyIdea.text: Translate revert reasons into clear guidance and recovery steps while avoiding raw internal errors.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Transaction Errors
Translation pattern
Capture low-level revert signals and present an explanation plus next steps. Keep messaging non-technical but specific enough to act on.
If revert reason contains allowance, show steps to approve token spending.
If user rejected the signature, explain that no on-chain change occurred and how to retry.
If unknown, provide troubleshooting steps: check balance, check gas, consult transaction history.
Example message
Transaction reverted: Insufficient allowance. To fix, approve token allowance in your wallet and try again. If unsure, check token balance and allowance settings.
Key Takeaway
Convert technical errors into clear steps the user can follow to recover.

screens.title: Loading data and historical events
screens.narratorSegment: Fetching contract data or historical events can take time and should be treated as part of the user journey. Define the design: show loading indicators and skeletons when initial data is being fetched, and present partial content where possible to reduce perceived latency. For example, load the latest event first and populate older events as they arrive. A key pattern is to show a small explanation like Loading contract state and a spinner, rather than leaving sections blank. A misconception is to render empty tables or placeholders without context; that makes users think the app is broken. Also consider caching or optimistic reads for frequently requested information to improve responsiveness. The practical takeaway is to provide visible progress, use skeletons or spinners, and allow users to continue interacting with non-dependent parts of the UI while data loads. This reduces anxiety and makes your app feel faster even when network calls are slow. Loading data and historical events means use spinners, skeletons, and progressive loading to keep users informed and reduce perceived latency.. In practical terms, keep users informed when reading blockchain data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Accessibility and security-focused UI
screens.narratorSegment: Accessibility and security considerations are essential when designing dApp interfaces. For accessibility, use semantic H T M L, provide text alternatives, ensure keyboard navigation, and maintain sufficient color contrast. A dApp user manages a wallet, pays gas, and waits for confirmations. These elements introduce delays and potential confusion, so your interface must provide clear guidance and prevent costly mistakes. We will look at state-driven rendering, feedback for pending and failed transactions, network mismatch handling, and accessibility considerations. For example, telling a user that a transaction is pending and disabling repeat actions prevents duplicate transactions and wasted gas. A common misconception is that web UI patterns alone are sufficient; in practice you must surface blockchain-specific status and educate without overwhelming the user. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design screens for disconnected, connected, wrong network, and pending transaction states, and implement clear visual and textual cues that reduce user risk. Think about the last time an app left you waiting without context; that frustration is amplified when money or irreversible actions are involved. How will you give your users confidence when the network is slow?

In this module you will master four practical skills that improve dApp usability. First, you will identify unique UX challenges in decentralized apps, such as wallet interactions, gas fees, and transaction latency, and explain why these require different patterns than typical web apps. Second, you will implement clear feedback mechanisms for transactions: how to show pending, confirmed, and failed states with useful messaging and transaction hashes. Third, you will design state-aware interfaces for disconnected, connected-but-no-account, wrong-network, and pending transaction conditions so users always know what to do next. Fourth, you will apply general UI and accessibility best practices, such as semantic markup, color contrast, and keyboard navigation, to make your dApp trustworthy and inclusive. Each objective is measurable: you will add conditional rendering for connection and network, display transaction status, and validate accessibility checks. These skills reduce user error, prevent lost funds, and increase confidence in your dApp. Which objective matters most for your current project, and how will you prioritize it?

This lesson is focused on translating UX objectives into concrete outcomes you can test. You should be able to explain three interface states clearly to a teammate and implement them in code: disconnected, wrong network, and pending transaction. For example, a disconnected state displays an explanation and a prominent connect affordance; a wrong network state explains the mismatch and offers an explicit path to resolve it; a pending transaction state disables repeat actions and shows a transaction hash. These are measurable behaviors you can test by disconnecting your wallet or switching the network. Accessibility and responsive design are also part of success: using semantic elements, sufficient contrast, and keyboard reachable controls ensures broader adoption. A common misconception is that polished visuals alone equal good UX. In truth, reliable state handling and clear messaging are what prevent user harm and build trust. After completing exercises, ask yourself: can a new user recover from a failed transaction without developer help?

Decentralized applications introduce UX challenges that are not common in traditional web apps. At the core, users must manage a separate wallet, contend with gas costs, and accept that transactions are sometimes slow and irreversible. Start by defining the core claim: a dApp interface must treat blockchain interactions as first-class events. Concretely, that means surfacing wallet connection status, transaction lifecycle, and network identity, and making recovery paths explicit. For example, a user who sends a token transfer expects feedback; if the UI does nothing for thirty seconds, the user may retry and create duplicate transfers. A common misconception is to rely on default wallet modals and assume they are always sufficient. In reality, you must complement wallet prompts with in-app messages and disabled actions to prevent mistakes. Design patterns include clear labels, confirmation steps for risky actions, and an activity log or transaction history. The practical takeaway is to always ask: what could go wrong from the user's perspective, and how does the interface prevent or recover from that failure? That mindset will reorganize your priorities and make your dApp safer.

Providing clear feedback during the transaction lifecycle is essential for user confidence. Describe the lifecycle: a transaction is initiated, sent to the network, may remain pending, then either confirms or reverts. For each stage, provide visual and textual cues. When pending, disable relevant controls, show a spinner, and display a short message with the transaction hash so the user can reference it. For confirmed transactions, show a success message with a green check and update the UI to reflect the new state. For failures, show a prominent error that explains why it failed when possible, for example insufficient allowance or user rejection. A concrete example: when a user updates a greeting on a contract, the UI should show Processing with a hash, then update the greeting on confirmation.
